title: Commercial Oil Production Begins in Cabinda
reason: Multiple independent sources converge on 1968, not 1971, as the year Gulf Oil (Cabinda Gulf Oil Company / CABGOC) began commercial oil production offshore Cabinda. Gulf made its offshore discovery at the Malongo field in 1966 and began extraction/first oil in 1968; by 1972 the company was extracting ~9 million tons/year and paying Portugal ~$400M annually in lease payments (60% of the Portuguese colonial war budget) — the CLA Journal academic paper states explicitly: 'In 1968 Gulf began extraction, and by 1972 the company was extracting 9 million tons of oil.' Separately, 1971 is documented as the year Gulf discovered the Takula field (a different, later Cabinda field) — not the start of commercial production. The country (Angola), operator (Gulf Oil), location (Cabinda offshore), and broader narrative (oil funding Portugal's colonial war, oil eventually eclipsing coffee) are all substantively correct — only the year is wrong, off by three years. This is a year error significant enough that the input year does not fall within a defensible tolerance of the well-documented 1968 start date.

title: Nationalization of Banks and Major Industries
reason: The MPLA government's nationalization of banks, industries, and agricultural estates in Angola is real, but it happened predominantly in 1975-1976, not 1977. Since no independent source places the described bundle of nationalizations (banks + insurance + industries + agricultural estates) concretely in 1977, and the core legislative/economic actions cluster in 1976 (with insurance trailing into 1978), the year as given is wrong. title: Mbanza Kongo Becomes Angola's First UNESCO World Heritage Site
reason: Confirmed from multiple independent sources. Mbanza Kongo (Vestiges of the Capital of the former Kingdom of Kongo) was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2017 during the 41st session of the World Heritage Committee held in Krakow, Poland (2-12 July 2017), per whc.unesco.org session records and CNN/africanews coverage. Multiple sources (africanews.com, allAfrica) explicitly confirm this was Angola's first World Heritage Site ("These are the first world heritage sites in Angola and Eritrea"). The site is confirmed as the former political/spiritual capital of the Kingdom of Kongo from the 14th-19th centuries, containing the ruins of the Cathedral of the Holy Saviour of Congo, plus royal-grounds structures tied to the Manikongo rulers - the Jalankuwo (judgment tree) and sunguilu (ritual site where the king's body was washed before burial), matching the description's "royal memorial and traditional judgment sites." The UNESCO citation language is confirmed nearly verbatim via search: "Mbanza Kongo illustrates, more than anywhere in sub-Saharan Africa, the profound changes caused by the introduction of Christianity and the arrival of the Portuguese into Central Africa" - matching the description's framing about Portuguese colonizers/Christianity. One minor unresolved detail: sources give differing construction dates for the cathedral (one source says built/initiated 1491, extended 1534-1549, elevated to cathedral status 1596; another news source (africanews) explicitly states "built in 1549" matching the event description verbatim), but this does not change the core, materially-confirmed facts of the event (year, country, first-UNESCO-site status, site identity, and significance).

title: Angola Restructures Chinese Debt Amid COVID-19 Crisis
reason: Independently corroborated across multiple non-off-limits sources: in June 2020 Angola secured a three-year moratorium/freeze on principal payments (~US$4.9B, running to Q2 2023) from Chinese lenders China Development Bank and ICBC, explicitly tied to the COVID-19-driven collapse in oil prices (Brent fell below $30/barrel in early 2020) compounding Angola's pre-existing oil-price recession (2016-2020). Angola's heavy exposure to Chinese creditors from post-civil-war infrastructure lending (~$42.6B borrowed 2000-2020, largest African borrower from China) is well documented by AidData/China Africa Research Initiative. Angola also implemented a strict COVID-19 lockdown in 2020 (national state of emergency declared March 27, 2020, with a national lockdown, closure of non-essential businesses, suspended public transport) that hit its already fragile, oil-dependent economy (GDP projected to shrink ~4.5% in 2020). All material details in the description (actors, timing, mechanism, causal link, lockdown) check out. Source used (SCMP) is independent and not on the off-limits list (only chathamhouse.org is excluded).
